body.text: The quickest way to identify a pure silk saree is to look for the Silk Mark, a small hologram tag that certifies pure natural silk. Many older and preloved sarees have no tag, so three home tests do most of the work. Tilt the saree under a light and watch for a sheen that shifts colour. Rub it between your palms and feel it warm. Burn one loose thread and smell for burning hair.
Art silk, polyester and blends can look convincing in a photograph and even in the hand. Here are seven checks, starting with the easiest.
Seven ways to check whether a silk saree is original
1. Look for the Silk Mark
The Silk Mark is India's certification for pure natural silk. It is run by the Silk Mark Organisation of India under the Central Silk Board, and it comes as a hologram label carrying a unique number.
A missing tag proves nothing on its own. Sarees bought before the scheme became common never had one, and tags are often cut off over the years. On a preloved saree, the other six tests matter more.
2. Watch how it catches the light

Hold the saree up and tilt it slowly under a lamp. Pure silk has a sheen that seems to change colour as the angle changes. Silk fibres are triangular, and they bend light the way a prism does. Art silk and polyester give a flat white shine that looks the same from every angle.
3. Rub it between your palms

Rub a section briskly between your hands for a few seconds. Silk grows warm. Polyester and rayon stay cool. Scrunch a fold close to your ear as well. Silk gives a faint rustle, and it springs back without feeling stiff or papery.
4. Burn one loose thread, and only one

This is the most reliable home test, and the one to treat with care. Burn a single stray thread from the fall or the very edge of the pallu, over a sink or a metal tray. Never test the body of the saree, and never a saree that is not yours.

**Pure silk** burns slowly, curls away from the flame and smells like burning hair, because silk is a protein, as hair is. The flame usually goes out on its own and leaves black ash that crumbles to powder.
**Polyester** melts and shrinks from the flame, smells of plastic, and leaves a hard bead you cannot crush.
**Rayon**, which is often sold as art silk, burns quickly like paper, smells like burning leaves and leaves soft grey ash.
5. Turn it over

Handwoven silk shows small irregularities in the weave, the marks of a person working a loom. On motif work, the pattern usually shows clearly on the reverse. A perfectly even weave with a blank back often points to a power loom and synthetic yarn.
6. Check the zari

Zari comes in three kinds, and they are priced very differently. **Pure zari** is fine silver coated in gold. **Tested zari** is copper coated in silver and then gold. **Metallic zari** is a coated plastic film.

To tell them apart, find a loose end of zari at the very edge and scrape the metal gently. Pure zari stays silver right through. Tested zari shows a reddish copper colour underneath. Metallic zari has no metal at all, only a thin film that shines. Held to a flame, pure and tested zari leave a fine metal thread behind, and metallic zari melts.

Age tells you something too. Pure zari darkens slowly and evenly over decades. Tested zari tends to darken in patches as the copper comes through. Metallic zari does not tarnish, but it loses its shine and frays.
Tested zari is not a fake. It is a respectable and widely used material. It simply is not pure zari, and it should not be priced as if it were.

body.text: 7. Let the price make you look harder

Pure silk is expensive to produce, and handwoven silk more so. A "pure Kanjeevaram" at a price that seems remarkable usually is not one. Price proves nothing on its own, but a surprisingly low one is a good reason to run the other six tests with care.
How to identify a pure Banarasi silk saree

Banarasi sarees are woven in and around Varanasi, and the name is protected by Geographical Indication status. Look for dense brocade, often with floral motifs drawn from Mughal design, and zari woven into the fabric itself.

Then turn it over. In a kadhwa Banarasi, each motif is woven in separately by hand, so the back looks almost as neat as the front. In a cutwork piece, you will see trimmed threads behind each motif. Either way, look for the small irregularities a hand leaves. A back that is perfectly uniform suggests a power loom.
This matters most when buying preloved Banarasi sarees online, where you are judging from photographs. Always ask to see the reverse.

images.alt: Reverse of a handwoven Banarasi saree showing the finishing behind each motif

body.text: How to identify a pure Kanjeevaram silk saree

Kanjeevaram sarees, also called Kanchipuram sarees, are woven in Tamil Nadu from heavy mulberry silk, and they also hold Geographical Indication status. The clearest sign is the korvai join. The body and the border are woven separately and interlocked on the loom, which is how the border can contrast so completely with the body. Run your fingers along the inner edge of the border and you can often feel the join.

A genuine Kanjeevaram is noticeably heavy. Temple borders, checks and traditional motifs are typical, and older pieces use pure zari. For more on where each weave comes from, see our guide to [Indian saree fabrics and weaves](/journal/indian-saree-fabrics-and-weaves).

images.alt: The korvai join where a Kanjeevaram border meets the body

body.text: How to check a preloved silk saree before buying online
Photographs can hide a great deal, so ask for more than the seller shows you.

items: A photograph taken in daylight, not only styled shots.
A close view of the zari along the border.
The fold lines, where old silk fails first.
How the seller confirmed the fibre, and whether a Silk Mark is present.

body.text: Then ask what happens if the saree arrives and is not as described. A seller who answers all of this plainly is one worth buying from. If the words preloved and second hand leave you unsure, our guide to [what preloved means](/journal/preloved-sarees-meaning) explains the difference.
What home tests cannot tell you

Home tests are a good guide. They will catch an obvious synthetic and give you confidence in a genuine piece, but they are not laboratory proof. If you are unsure about an expensive saree, testing is available through the Silk Mark Organisation of India.
It is also why the seller matters. At From The Trunk, every saree is authenticated before it is listed, so the question of what it is has been answered before you ever see it.

items.question: How can I check if my silk saree is original at home?
items.answer: Tilt it under a light and look for a sheen that shifts colour. Rub it between your palms and feel it warm. Burn one loose thread and smell for burning hair. Pure silk passes all three.

items.question: Does every pure silk saree have a Silk Mark?
items.answer: No. Many were made before the scheme was common, and tags are often removed over time. A missing tag on an older saree is normal.

items.question: What is the difference between pure silk and art silk?
items.answer: Pure silk is a natural protein fibre spun by silkworms. Art silk, short for artificial silk, is usually rayon made from wood pulp, and sometimes polyester. It costs less, feels cooler to the touch and burns like paper.

items.question: How can I tell if zari is real?
items.answer: Gently scrape a loose end at the edge. Pure zari stays silver right through. Tested zari shows copper underneath. Metallic zari has no metal at all, only a shiny film.

items.question: Is the burn test safe for a silk saree?
items.answer: It is safe if you test a single loose thread from the fall or the edge of the pallu, over a sink or a metal tray. Never burn any part of the saree itself.
